title: The Mouse That Sees With Its Face
blurb: The little gray animal that reads a dark room with its whiskers, and quietly moved into human houses fifteen thousand years ago.

blocks.prompt: The Mouse in the Dark
blocks.text: A mouse has a secret. It cannot see very well. The dark does not stop it. The mouse has long whiskers on both sides of its nose. It sweeps them back and forth, very fast. The whiskers touch the wall. They touch the floor. They tell the mouse where to go. A mouse can squeeze through a hole as small as a pencil. If its head fits, the rest of it fits too. Then it finds a quiet corner, builds a soft nest out of bits of paper and grass, and sleeps all day.

blocks.prompt: The Teeth That Never Stop
blocks.text:
A mouse's front teeth never stop growing. They push up out of the jaw a little more every day, all through the mouse's life. That sounds like a problem, and it would be, except a mouse gnaws. It chews on seeds, on nutshells, on wood, on cardboard. Every bite grinds the tips of those teeth back down. The word rodent comes from an old word that means to gnaw, and mice are rodents. So are rats, squirrels, and beavers.

The front teeth are shaped for the job. The front of each tooth is covered in hard enamel. The back of it is softer. The soft part wears away faster, so the tooth keeps a sharp edge, like a chisel that sharpens itself.

Behind those front teeth there is a gap, right where a dog or a cat would have long pointy teeth. A mouse has none. It does not need them. A mouse is not hunting anything. It is looking for a seed.

answers: they keep growing out of the jaw
chewing grinds the tips of the teeth back down
the back, because it is softer
(inference: it eats seeds and plants, so it never has to catch or hold prey)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About thirty long whiskers on each side
It sweeps them ten times a second
Whiskers measure a gap before it squeezes in

blocks.prompt: Reading the Room in the Dark
blocks.text:
Sit in a dark room and you will feel useless. A mouse in a dark room is at work.

A mouse's eyes are not much help. They sit high on the sides of its head, good for catching a shadow swooping down, poor for detail. The real instrument is on its face. A house mouse has about thirty long whiskers arranged in neat rows on either side of its nose, and they are not decoration. Each whisker is rooted in a pocket packed with nerve endings. When a mouse explores, it sweeps those whiskers forward and back roughly ten times a second, brushing the wall, the floor, the edge of a gap. Out of that brushing it builds a picture of a room it has never seen.

This is why a mouse hugs the wall instead of crossing the open middle of a floor. The wall is information. The middle is nothing but risk.

The whiskers also do the measuring. A house mouse can pass through an opening barely wider than a pencil, because its skeleton is loose and its skull is the only truly rigid part of it. If the head fits, the mouse fits. Rather than guess, it touches the edge of the gap first and lets its whiskers report the width. Then it goes.

The nose finishes the job. A mouse leaves faint scent marks as it travels, so the paths it has already tested stay marked for next time. Whiskers for the shape of the world, scent for the memory of it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Mus musculus, the house mouse
Moved in with the first grain stores
Now on every continent but Antarctica
Male mice sing above human hearing
Songs found only by slowing recordings down
A partnership about fifteen thousand years old

blocks.prompt: The Animal That Moved In
blocks.text:
The house mouse did not always live in houses. For most of its history it was a small brown seed eater on dry ground somewhere around northern India and the hills of the Middle East, and there was nothing remarkable about it at all.

Then people stopped moving. Around fifteen thousand years ago, villages in the Fertile Crescent began gathering wild grain, storing it in one place, and staying near it through the year. A permanent pile of seed, under a roof, warm, guarded from owls and foxes: for a mouse, this was the best offer in the history of mice. The bold ones moved in. The nervous ones stayed outside and stayed ordinary. Archaeologists can track the switch in the bones they dig out of those old villages, because the mice that took the deal changed over generations, and their teeth changed along with their diet.

Everywhere people went afterward, the house mouse went too. It rode grain ships and wagons and freight containers into Europe, Africa, the Americas, and almost every island with a harbor. It now lives on every continent except Antarctica. It did not conquer anything. It followed the food and let us do the traveling.

There is one more thing worth knowing, and most people never hear it, in the most literal sense. Male house mice sing. Not squeaks: real songs, with repeated phrases and a clear structure, delivered at frequencies far above the range of human hearing. A mouse can sing under your kitchen floor at full volume and you will not catch a note of it. Scientists only found the songs by recording them and slowing the recordings down until they dropped into the range our ears can reach.

So we call it a pest, set traps for it, and share our buildings with it anyway. Fifteen thousand years is a long partnership. The odd part is that it was our idea first. We built the storehouse. The mouse only answered.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Whiskers sit in a grid, named by row and column
Whisking: about ten sweeps a second
Barrel cortex: one cell bundle per whisker
Mouse genome published in 2002
Almost every human gene has a mouse counterpart
The most studied mammal on Earth

blocks.prompt: The Mouse That Sees With Its Face
blocks.text:
Somewhere in the wall of your house, in total darkness, a mouse is building an accurate map of a room it cannot see. It is doing this with its face.

Start with the equipment. Along either side of a house mouse's snout sit rows of long, stiff whiskers, roughly thirty of the big ones per side, arranged in a grid so regular that researchers identify each one by its row and column. A whisker itself is dead material, like your hair, and feels nothing at all. The sensing happens at the root, where each whisker sits in a follicle wrapped in hundreds of nerve fibers that register the smallest bend.

Now watch the mouse use them. It does not simply let its whiskers drag against things. It drives them, sweeping the whole array forward and back about ten times a second, a behavior called whisking. Contact bends the whisker, the follicle reports the bend, and out of thousands of these tiny reports the animal assembles width, texture, distance, and shape. In a laboratory, a mouse can tell a rough surface from a slightly less rough one using a single whisker, in the dark, faster than you could decide with your eyes.

The strange part is what this does to the brain. Cut a thin slice of a mouse's sensory cortex, stain it, and put it under a microscope, and a map of the animal's face stares back at you. The cells are gathered into small oval bundles, one bundle per whisker, laid out in the same rows and columns as the whiskers themselves. Neuroscientists call them barrels. Take away a single whisker follicle in a newborn mouse and its barrel never forms properly, while the neighboring barrels spread into the territory it should have claimed. The face is written into the brain, and the writing responds to what actually happens to the animal.

That last fact is a large part of why the mouse became the most studied mammal on Earth. The barrel field handed researchers something rare: a sense organ with a visible, countable, one-to-one map in the cortex, sitting in an animal that is small, breeds quickly, and shares the overwhelming majority of its genes with us. When the mouse genome was published in 2002, it turned out that almost every human gene had a recognizable mouse counterpart. Mice and rats now make up roughly nine out of every ten animals used in biomedical research, and much of what we know about how brains learn, how bodies fight infection, and how cancers begin was learned first from them.

It is worth sitting with the whole shape of that. The same animal people trap in their kitchens and dismiss as vermin is the one that agriculture accidentally invited indoors fifteen thousand years ago, and the one on which a great deal of modern medicine now rests. Being small and unremarkable turned out to be an extraordinary strategy. It got the mouse in everywhere, including the laboratory that studies it.

Whatever you make of that bargain, the mouse in the wall is not lost. It knows exactly where it is. It is reading the wall with its face, ten times a second, and it does not need the light on.
